claims.claim: Eight instances, each substantiated.
claims.evidence: 14.1 through 14.8 are present and numbered. Of the eight, four stand as written, one is partly closed (14.4), and three are stale (14.2, 14.6, 14.7). The count is right; three of the eight descriptions are not.

claims.claim: The unreadable daemon token: the caller reports "daemon unreachable" and proceeds, while the daemon is alive and heartbeating, so the off-box dead-man never fires.
claims.evidence: The fail-open and the dead-man gap hold: the class is HookFailureInterventionUnavailable → FailClosed:false (ai_failure_resolver.go:93-98), a 401 is produced by daemon_auth.go:344, and /health still answers 200 (server.go:1359-1367). Group membership is best-effort: install-scripts/production/install.sh:435-439 uses `usermod -aG ... || true`, `gpasswd -a ... || true`, `adduser ... || true`. BUT the human-visible half is already fixed: cmd/devoid/ai_failure_resolver.go:284-296 calls daemon.ReadTokenDetailed and, on TokenUnreadable, prints a DIFFERENT sentence naming the token path, 'permission denied', and 'The daemon may well be running; starting it again will not help.' That branch predates this document (present at base commit 002e2cfd).
claims.correctedText: **14.1 The unreadable daemon token — the worst one.** On a machine install whose interactive user is not in the product's group, the daemon answers its health check in 14 ms, the capability token cannot be read, every request goes out unauthenticated, the daemon returns 401, and the caller **proceeds** — while the daemon is alive and heartbeating, so the off-box dead-man alarm never fires either. The group membership is added on a best-effort basis at install (`usermod || true`). The *stderr notice* now separates the two causes and names the token path and the remedy; what has not changed is that the checkpoint is not evaluated, that the internal reason bucket still reads `daemon-unreachable-*`, and that nothing off-box distinguishes this from a healthy endpoint.

claims.claim: The daemon is a scheduled task with no service control-manager registration, no security descriptor, no failure/recovery configuration, and no watchdog; because the trigger is "at startup" there is no restart after a crash until reboot.
claims.evidence: Three of the five sub-claims are false as written. (1) Failure/recovery EXISTS on two of the three registration paths: install-scripts/production/install.ps1:2921-2926 sets `-RestartCount 3 -RestartInterval (New-TimeSpan -Minutes 1)`, and internal/daemon/persistence_windows.go:230-233 emits `<RestartOnFailure><Interval>PT1M</Interval><Count>3</Count></RestartOnFailure>`. (2) A WATCHDOG exists: internal/daemon/server.go:2178 and :2186 call ensureDaemonPersistence on start and on every tick of a 5-minute ticker (aiWireReconcileInterval, server.go:2140), which re-registers a missing or misconfigured task and writes a high-severity `daemon_persistence_recreated` bypass event (internal/daemon/persistence.go:186-194). (3) The MSI path is the one that has NO restart config: CA_InstallDaemonTask runs `devoid.exe setup install-daemon` (CustomActions.wxs:179), which uses plain `schtasks /Create /F /TN .. /SC ONSTART /RU SYSTEM /RL HIGHEST` (cmd/devoid/setup_installer.go:853-859) — and plain /Create cannot express RestartOnFailure. The reconciler will never repair it: taskInfo.configuredFor (internal/daemon/persistence.go:66-86) inspects exists/boot-trigger/SYSTEM/HighestAvailable/command/arguments and NEVER inspects RestartOnFailure. What remains true: no SCM registration, no security descriptor, and the same `schtasks /Delete /TN <name> /F` the product itself uses (cmd/devoid/main.go:2697) removes it.
claims.correctedText: **14.2 The daemon is not a Windows service.** It is a scheduled task (`/SC ONSTART /RU SYSTEM /RL HIGHEST`). There is no service control-manager registration and no security descriptor on it, and any local **administrator** can delete it with the same command the product itself uses (`schtasks /Delete /TN "Devoid Daemon" /F`, `cmd/devoid/main.go:2697`). Two things that WERE listed here are no longer true, and the third is now narrower. **Failure recovery exists on two of the three registration paths** — `install.ps1:2921-2926` sets `-RestartCount 3 -RestartInterval 1m`, and the daemon's own XML re-registration carries `RestartOnFailure Count=3 Interval=PT1M` (`internal/daemon/persistence_windows.go:230-233`). **A watchdog exists** — `ensureDaemonPersistence` runs at start and every 5 minutes (`server.go:2178,2186`), re-registers a deleted or misconfigured task, and emits a high-severity `daemon_persistence_recreated` event. It is an *in-process* watchdog, so it cannot run while the daemon is dead: deleting the task with the daemon stopped is permanent until the next start. **The MSI path still has no restart configuration at all** — `CA_InstallDaemonTask` shells out to `setup install-daemon`, which uses plain `schtasks /Create` (`cmd/devoid/setup_installer.go:853-859`), and plain `/Create` cannot set restart-on-failure. `taskInfo.configuredFor` (`persistence.go:66-86`) never inspects `RestartOnFailure`, so the reconciler judges that task "present" and never upgrades it. **MSI-installed endpoints therefore have no crash recovery; script-installed endpoints do.**

claims.correctedText: **14.4 The hook status command — the Claude half is closed, the Codex half is not.** *Closed 2026-08-27 (Installers `40f34362`, agent 7.10.6): on the Claude lane the undecided count now rides the primary verdict line in every state including a measured zero, the vendor-discard count reaches that same line, and a non-zero count (or an unmeasurable counter) turns the `[OK]` into `[!] ... UNGOVERNED Claude Code invocations` and a non-zero exit —* `cmd/devoid/ai.go:447-504`, `:723-735`. **What remains:** the Codex lane still prints both numbers as footnotes and throws them away. `ai_codex_hooks.go:508` and `:513` discard their return values, and `printCodexObservedAndVerdict` (`ai_codex_lanes.go:189-395`) composes its verdict from the fired/applicable count and the two lane-attestability flags only. `[devoid] [OK] Codex managed controls installed + compliant` can therefore still stand over a non-zero undecided count. The footnote printer also still returns early on a measured zero (`ai.go:701-710`), so on the Codex lane silence and nought remain indistinguishable.

claims.claim: The transport route indicator printed "anthropic: NEVER OBSERVED" after a request demonstrably travelled that route; the indicator is contradicted by the traffic.
claims.evidence: The indicator is not contradicted by the traffic — it measures a different thing, and it is correctly wired. recordTransportRouteDecision (internal/daemon/ai_transport_observation.go:60) is called from recordAIProxyAlert (internal/daemon/ai_handlers.go:2360), which is the AlertObserver wired at server.go:712 and openai_wire.go:113. It increments on every proxy DECISION. It cannot increment on traffic that produces no decision, and most traffic produces none: isAIScanTarget (internal/proxy/ai_proxy.go:1274-1277) admits only POST to `/v1/messages` and `/v1/messages/count_tokens`; everything else takes `h.forward(w, r, nil)` at :320-324 with no emitAlert call anywhere on that path. The §15 register row (L931) says the same thing in the other direction — 'no decision was recorded anywhere' — which is the honest finding.
claims.correctedText: **14.5 The transport route indicator counts decisions, not traffic.** The row reads `NEVER OBSERVED` until the route has carried a *decision*, and the counter behind it is correctly wired (`recordTransportRouteDecision`, `internal/daemon/ai_transport_observation.go:60`, called from the proxy AlertObserver at `ai_handlers.go:2360`). The gap is that only a POST to `/v1/messages` or `/v1/messages/count_tokens` is ever scanned (`internal/proxy/ai_proxy.go:1274-1277`); every other method and path is forwarded transparently at `:320-324` with no alert and therefore no observation. So a request can demonstrably travel the route and leave the indicator at NEVER OBSERVED — not because the indicator is wrong, but because *nothing decided anything*. The label is what misleads: it reads as a statement about traffic and is a statement about verdicts.

Saying so here matters because the liveproof register entry for item 101 [H1], written 2026-08-07, still records "NO PRODUCTION FILE CARRIES THAT DESCRIPTOR YET" — true when written, stale since.' The writer is hardenMachineEndpointIdentity at internal/core/config/endpoint_identity_windows.go:30-32 → winacl.HardenMachineSecret. The rest stands: credentials.json (credentials_atomic_windows.go:19,63) and the daemon token (internal/daemon/daemon_token_perm_windows.go:17 → winacl.HardenMachineLocalRead) both sit on MachineLocalReadSDDL = 'O:SYG:SYD:P(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)(A;;0x120089;;;BU)' — a BUILTIN\Users FILE_GENERIC_READ ACE. claims.correctedText: **14.6 The machine-secret ACL.** The restrictive descriptor is `MachineSecretSDDL = "O:SYG:SYD:P(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)"` — SYSTEM and Administrators only, no `BUILTIN\Users` ACE. *Closed in part 2026-08-18: exactly one production file now carries it — `endpoint-identity.json`, the endpoint signing private key, written through `hardenMachineEndpointIdentity` (`internal/core/config/endpoint_identity_windows.go:30-32`), pinned by `winacl.TestMachineDescriptorRouting`.* **Still open:** the credentials file and the daemon token remain on `MachineLocalReadSDDL`, which grants `BUILTIN\Users` `FILE_GENERIC_READ` (`0x120089`) — readable by every local user. It cannot simply be narrowed: `attachDaemonToken` reads the machine token in the non-elevated user's context on every shim and every `devoid ai hook` invocation, and tightening it would 401 every non-elevated package install fleet-wide. The precondition is a per-user credential split that does not exist yet (`internal/daemon/daemon_token_perm_windows.go:9-16`, `internal/winacl/machine_secret_windows.go:71-91`).

omissions.what: The destructive-rm hard block: an unrelaxable block on every `rm -rf ~/<anything>` and `rm -rf $HOME/<anything>`.
omissions.whyItMatters: It is the most customer-visible fact about the product today and it is absent from the whole document. Three separate mechanisms combine into it, and each is individually documented while the combination is not: (1) the shipped regex treats any home-relative path as a "broad target"; (2) `destructive-rm` is a malicious-floor member at `minimumDisposition: 'block'`; (3) since Backend PR #285 / ECS td 322 the floor holds on the READ path, so the raise is applied to every policy pull for every tenant. The consequence is that a developer's agent cannot run `rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache` or `rm -rf $HOME/.cache/pip`, and no administrator on any tenant can relax it from the console — the stored value is raised back to `block` at serve time. The D4 default table says `warn`, so an operator reading the constants will conclude the opposite of what ships.
omissions.evidence: COMPILED THE SHIPPED REGEX AND RAN IT. Installers@5b129523 internal/toolrisk/toolrisk.go:121-122, pattern `\brm\s+(?:-[a-zA-Z]*\s+)*-?[rf]{1,2}[a-zA-Z]*\s+(?:-[a-zA-Z]+\s+)*(?:/\s*$|/\s+|/\*|~(?:/\S*)?|\$HOME\b|\.{1,2}\s*$|\*\s*$|/(?:etc|usr|var|bin|boot|lib|lib64|sbin|opt|root|home|sys|proc|dev)\b)`. Results — TRUE: `rm -rf $HOME/.cache/pip`, `rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache`, `rm -rf $HOME/projects/scratch`, `rm -rf ~/dev/myapp/node_modules`, `rm -rf ~/Downloads/tmp`, `rm -rf /var/log/foo`. FALSE: `rm -rf ./build`, `rm -rf /tmp/mybuild`, `rm -rf build/`, `rm -rf node_modules`, `rm -rf ../sibling`. The alternative that does it is `~(?:/\S*)?`, plus `\$HOME\b` which matches the prefix of `$HOME/anything`. Floor membership: Backend/src/ai-security-policy/ai-malicious-floor.ts:155 via `destructive()` at :104-109 (`minimumDisposition: 'block'`). Read-path enforcement: ai-security-policy.service.ts:2198. D4 default: ai-security-policy.constants.ts:1238 (`'destructive-rm': 'warn', // system paths`), and the comment at :1330-1341 still describes the raise as happening only on the WRITE path via `applyMaliciousFloor` in `buildRiskGroupUpdateDto` — that comment is now itself stale. Bonus false negative from the same compile: `rm -rf /tmp/x ~/.cache` returns FALSE, because only the first target after the flags is inspected.
omissions.proposedText:
### 17.1 The destructive-rm hard block — the most customer-visible defect today

**What a customer sees.** An agent session cannot run `rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache`, `rm -rf $HOME/.cache/pip`, or `rm -rf ~/dev/myapp/node_modules`. Each is refused as `destructive-rm`. `rm -rf ./build` and `rm -rf /tmp/mybuild` are fine.

**Why.** Three correct-in-isolation decisions compose into it.

1. The shipped rule treats *any* home-relative path as a broad target. The alternation is `~(?:/\S*)?` and `\$HOME\b` — `internal/toolrisk/toolrisk.go:122`. The comment two lines above says "Narrow `rm -rf ./build` does NOT match (the target must be broad)", which is true and is not the case that fires. **Compiled and run 2026-08-28**: true for `rm -rf $HOME/.cache/pip`, `rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache`, `rm -rf $HOME/projects/scratch`; false for `rm -rf ./build`, `rm -rf /tmp/mybuild`.
2. `destructive-rm` is a malicious-floor member at `minimumDisposition: 'block'` — `ai-malicious-floor.ts:155`, `:104-109`.
3. Since Backend PR #285 (ECS td 322) the floor holds on the **read** path: `withMaliciousFloorApplied` is the first statement of `assembleEffectiveDto` (`ai-security-policy.service.ts:2198`).

**Therefore no administrator on any tenant can relax it.** Setting `toolRisk.destructive-rm` to `warn` or `monitor` in the console stores that value and the endpoint is served `block` on the very next pull, with a warn line in the server log and nothing in the console explaining the divergence.

**The D4 default table says `warn`** (`ai-security-policy.constants.ts:1238`), so the constants and the wire disagree by design. The comment at `:1330-1341` still describes the raise as happening on the write path only; that is now stale.

**A false negative in the same rule, worth knowing:** only the first target after the flags is inspected, so `rm -rf /tmp/x ~/.cache` does **not** fire.

**The decision is a product decision, not a bug fix.** Either narrow the rule so a path under `$HOME` is not automatically broad, or lower `destructive-rm` beneath the floor in `ai-malicious-floor.ts`. Doing the second alone leaves the detector firing at `warn` fleet-wide; doing the first alone leaves the floor correct and the detector honest. Do not "fix" it by editing the D4 table — the floor overrides it.

omissions.what: A clean MSI uninstall leaves the entire `C:\ProgramData\devoid\bin` payload on disk, and the reason is not harden-shims.
omissions.whyItMatters: It is residue, not exposure — the ACL is correct and PATH is cleaned, so nothing intercepts — but it is 41 files and roughly 424 MB per machine that never goes away, including executables named `claude.exe`, `codex.exe` and `npm.exe`, on every endpoint that has ever had an earlier DeVoid MSI installed. More importantly, the causal story matters: the proposed explanation ("harden-shims has no uninstall counterpart") is wrong, and acting on it would fix nothing.
omissions.evidence: PROVEN from the 2026-08-27 real-box uninstall log, cross-checked against the .wxs. The MSI log records `Disallowing uninstallation of component: {GUID} since another client exists` 63 times, including `{A1C7D3E9-4B62-4F18-9E2A-7C5B0D4F8A13}` (comp_claude_exe) and `{B2D8E4FA-5C73-4A29-8F3B-6D4C1E5A9B24}` (comp_codex_exe) — the exact GUIDs at windows-installer/msi-build/Product.wxs:235,239. Consequence: with `REMOVE=ALL` and features `CoreAgent` and `DependencyShims` both resolving `Action: Absent`, ALL 79 components resolved to `Action: Null` (only 4 got `Action: Absent`, all the Firefox-policy-removed pair). `RemoveFiles` and `RemoveFolders` both ran in 0 ms and returned 1 having deleted nothing. The unregister ops carry `PreviouslyPinned=1`. The .wxs is not at fault: `Permanent="no"` (Product.wxs:376), and at install the components registered with `SharedDllRefCount=0`. Sizing: Product.wxs has 43 `<File Id=` rows, of which 2 are browser native-messaging manifests that live outside BINDIR → 41 files in BINDIR, and 20 of them are separate copies of `devoid.exe` (plus `devoid-daemon.exe` and `devoid-prompt-guard-host.exe`), which is where ~424 MB comes from. harden-shims is not implicated: it only re-applies ACLs to files already present (cmd/devoid/main.go:8370-8386 → security.HardenShimDirectory, internal/security/shim_hardening.go:14-32), it creates nothing, and MSI never reached the delete step.
omissions.proposedText:
### 17.2 A clean uninstall leaves the whole bin payload behind

**Observed 2026-08-27 on a real Windows box.** Install and uninstall both exit 0, every user config file restores byte-identical, PATH is cleaned, and the ACL on what remains is correct — so **nothing intercepts anything**. But `C:\ProgramData\devoid\bin` still holds **41 files, roughly 424 MB**, including executables named `claude.exe`, `codex.exe` and `npm.exe`. It is residue, not exposure.

**The cause is MSI component ownership, not a missing custom action.** The uninstall log records `Disallowing uninstallation of component: {…} since another client exists` **63 times** — including the exact GUIDs of `comp_claude_exe` and `comp_codex_exe` from `Product.wxs:235,239`. With `REMOVE=ALL` and both features resolving `Action: Absent`, every one of the 79 components still resolved to `Action: Null`; `RemoveFiles` and `RemoveFolders` each ran in 0 ms and deleted nothing. The unregister ops carry `PreviouslyPinned=1`.

"Another client" means an **earlier DeVoid ProductCode is still registered against the same ComponentIds** under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\Installer\Components`. So any machine that has ever carried a previous DeVoid MSI uninstalls to a full bin directory, and a fresh machine does not. The `.wxs` is innocent: components are `Permanent="no"` (`Product.wxs:376`) and register with `SharedDllRefCount=0` at install.

**41 files / ~424 MB is exactly the MSI's own BINDIR payload**: 43 `<File>` rows minus the 2 browser native-messaging manifests that live elsewhere, and 20 of the 41 are separate copies of `devoid.exe`.

**`harden-shims` is not the cause.** It re-applies ACLs to files already on disk (`cmd/devoid/main.go:8370-8386`); it creates nothing, and MSI never reached a delete step for it to have undone. A teardown custom action would work, but the root fix is component-ownership hygiene across ProductCodes.

reorganisation:
Part III is structurally sound and should keep its shape; three targeted changes would make it hold its value as things get fixed.

**1. Give §16 a dated closed block, and start using it.** The document's own editing rule already demands this and §16 is the only list that has outgrown it — three of its fourteen entries moved state in the twenty-four hours before this audit and nothing distinguishes them from the eleven that did not. The proposed block is in the omissions above. Do the same in §14.4, §14.6 and §14.7, where the closure is partial and the *remainder* is the finding: each should read as "closed <date>: <what changed, with the commit>. What remains: <the narrower, still-true fact>." That format is what stops a half-fix from reading as a whole one, which is the failure mode this section exists to prevent.

**2. Split §17 into two lists, because it currently mixes two questions.** Items 1-6 answer "is this fleet protected right now" and items 7-10 answer "what does the product claim that it cannot back up". They deserve different urgency and different readers. With the destructive-rm block added, the first list is also no longer only about gaps in coverage — it now contains a control that is working *too hard* and cannot be tuned, which is a different kind of customer harm and belongs at the top precisely because it is the one a customer notices today. Add the file:line anchors; §17 is the one section with no citations and therefore the one most likely to rot.

**3. Add §17.1 and §17.2 as full subsections rather than list items.** Both need more than a line: the destructive-rm block is a three-mechanism composition where each part is individually correct, and the uninstall residue has a proposed cause that is *wrong* and a proven cause that is not obvious. A one-line entry for either would be re-derived incorrectly by the next reader — which is exactly what happened to the harden-shims explanation.

Two cross-cutting notes.

*On §15:* the register now disagrees with §14.6 in a way the code itself has already flagged. `internal/winacl/machine_secret_windows.go:63-69` names the register's machine-secret quarantine reason as stale and dates the change (2026-08-18). When a source file goes to the trouble of saying "this document is out of date about me", that is the highest-quality staleness signal available, and it is worth a standing habit: before trusting a §15 quarantine reason, grep the named package for the entry id.

*On the two live proofs that landed 2026-08-27:* both were taken on sandboxed rigs against a **local** Backend or with the backend pinned to a dead loopback port, and the pre-tool-deny proof records that "the deciding authority was the endpoint's LOCAL floor, not server policy". The register's evidence blocks say this plainly; §15's table currently does not. Whatever wording the table adopts, it should carry that qualifier, because three observed entries all resting on the local floor is a materially weaker statement than three entries resting on server policy, and the difference is exactly what §13.3 is about.
